transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hale (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Aurora - Partnerships), Marcus Yang (Aurora - GPU Lead), Anika Bose (Aurora - SRE)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, done a quick intro — I'm the AE covering partners. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Lena: Hi Jordan, hi Priya. Good, thanks. Excited to chat — quick note, apologies if the audio is a little rough, we're on a plane wifi earlier so may drop.
[00:12] Priya: No worries, we got you. Do you want me to start with a 3-minute about Redwood's partner model and the Dedicated/Private options then go into technical fit?
[00:18] Lena: That sounds good. Marcus will jump in on the GPU specifics.
[00:21] Marcus: Yep, happy to.

Summary (auto): Intro + discovery to evaluate integration possibilities between Aurora's managed GPU pools and Redwood's serving/runtime. Discussed architecture patterns: co-located dedicated pools, private control plane in VPC, or hybrid routing. Raised security and compliance requirements; agreed to run a joint benchmark pilot.

[00:40] Priya: Cool. So high level — Redwood provides three primary modes: hosted API if you want the fastest time to value; Dedicated which is reserved GPU capacity we run for customers or partners; and Private which is a customer-controlled control plane in their VPC or on-prem. For partners like you, we usually explore two angles: one, you surface Redwood as a managed inference option on top of your GPU marketplace; two, we co-run Dedicated pools on your hardware under a revenue-share or reseller model.
[01:05] Marcus: And from our side, we're trying to figure out if we expose our fleet as raw instances, or if we want Redwood to run a control plane that schedules across our pools. What's the network hit like for Private? If the control plane sits in our VPC does that mean egress for telemetry?
[01:22] Priya: Good question. For Redwood Private, the control plane can be customer-hosted in the VPC — only the orchestration plane needs limited outgoing connections for telemetry/updates unless you opt for fully air-gapped. We can support a no-egress model with a periodic offline sync but that requires additional entitlements. Telemetry can be routed to your internal ingest via S3 or on-prem collectors. There is some tradeoff — less telemetry means less automatic routing intelligence.
[01:45] Lena: Got it. On the security side, SOC2 is table stakes for our enterprise customers. Also we have strict KMS policies — any key management needs to be under our HSM. Can Redwood integrate with customer KMS/HSM?
[01:58] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integration, and Dedicated can be configured to encrypt model artifacts at rest with your keys. We have an audit log stream that can push to your SIEM or S3.
[02:10] Anika: Quick clarifying question — when you say Dedicated you run the actual inference runtime on the partner hardware or is it in Redwood's datacenter?
[02:18] Priya: Both are possible models. Often Dedicated means reserved capacity in our cloud under contract. But for partners, we offer a co-located model where Redwood's runtime is deployed onto partner-managed nodes as a managed tenant. That way we get the kernel optimizations, batching, and model lifecycle, while you provide the GPU.
[02:33] Marcus: Okay that helps. On hardware we run A100s predominantly, some H100s in newer racks. We also have multi-tenant partitioning via MIG for some customers. Does Redwood support MIG/partitioned GPUs?
[02:46] Priya: We do have support for MIG on specific model families, though perf characteristics differ. For high throughput generation workloads we typically recommend full-device allocations for KV-cache heavy tasks; MIG is great for many smaller embedding workloads. We'll detail perf regressions in the benchmark plan.
[02:58] Marcus: And what about quantization? A lot of our customers prefer INT8 quantized models to reduce footprint.
[03:04] Priya: Our runtime supports quantized execution paths and can choose kernels based on quantization profile. One caveat — some open models exhibit quality differences when aggressively quantized — we recommend running evals on your prompt sets as part of pilot.

[03:20] [00:03:20] Lena: Switching gears — commercial. What does a pilot typically look like in terms of cost split and lead time?
[03:28] Jordan: Pilots are flexible. We've done 1-month pilots where the partner covers the GPU costs and Redwood covers the orchestration and engineering support. For a revenue share, we usually negotiate percentages based on support and go-to-market contribution. Lead time for a pilot with access to hardware and networking is usually two weeks to stand up a baseline cluster and run initial benchmarks.
[03:47] Marcus: Two weeks is tight but plausible. We'll need to coordinate networking — do we need to open specific ports or is it all over standard TLS?
[03:55] Priya: Most traffic is TLS to the control plane; for the data-path we use gRPC/TLS over standard ports. For private peering we can put everything on a direct VPC peering connection. We'll share a network diagram.

[04:10] Marcus: On the performance side we care about 95th percentile latency for short generation (<=256 tokens) under concurrency. Any ballpark numbers you can share for A100?
[04:21] Priya: Ballpark: for an A100 with optimized kernels and batch size tuned, you can see single-request latencies in the 40-120ms range for small completions, but it depends heavily on model size, KV cache hit rate, and batch mixing. Embeddings and reranking are typically lower. We'll run your exact model/seqlen mix in the benchmark.
[04:39] Anika: A note — our customers will ask about data residency and logs. Can Redwood avoid storing user prompt content at rest?
[04:47] Jordan: Yes, we support configurations where request/response payloads are not stored or are redacted at the tokenization layer. We also have configurable retention on audit logs.

[04:58] Lena: In terms of integrations, we're also exploring if we can offer Redwood as a white-label inference option inside our marketplace for SI partners. That ties into billing and metering — how granular is Redwood's usage reporting?
[05:10] Jordan: We provide token-level and request-level metering, and our console exposes per-route, per-model cost and latency breakdowns. For partners we can produce usage reports per account or per tenant which you can ingest into your billing system (CSV or API).
[05:24] Marcus: You mentioned automatic fallback and graceful degradation earlier in docs we skimmed. If a node fails, will traffic get routed automatically to another variant?
[05:33] Priya: Yes — smart routing policies can failover by model variant or region. For partner-deployed Dedicated pools we can configure automatic fallback to a hosted Redwood pool if you opt in. That is a business decision though, because hosted fallback would mean cross-account data movement unless redaction is enabled.

[05:51] Jordan: There's sometimes confusion around KV cache and prefix caching. Marcus, I think you asked about reuse of cached tokens across requests?
[05:59] Marcus: Right, if a lot of our workloads are chatty/interactive, how does caching hit rate look?
[06:05] Priya: We support prefix caching and session-aware KV caches. The hit rate will hinge on prompt patterns. As part of the benchmark we'll instrument and estimate cost savings from caching.

[06:15] [06:15] Marcus: One more infra nuance — we have a customer who requires mutual TLS between services; can Redwood support mTLS for service-to-service?
[06:23] Priya: Yes, we can configure mTLS for service endpoints and integrate with your internal CA.

[06:28] Lena: Legal question for Jordan — what does a partnership MOU typically include? Are there NDAs first?
[06:34] Jordan: Typically we start with an NDA, then an MOU outlining pilot scope, responsibilities, data ownership, and a non-binding revenue share framework. Lena, if you want I can draft a one-page MOU and have our legal teams iterate.

[06:46] Lena: Please do. We'll also want to see SOC2 docs — do you have an external link or a redacted bundle?
[06:52] Jordan: We can share SOC2 Type II and our security package — I'll send the partner pack link.

[06:58] Marcus: For the tech deep dive I'd like to include our storage and networking engineer. We use a disaggregated NVMe layer with a high-bandwidth RDMA fabric — wonder how much throughput Redwood expects for KV cache misses.
[07:09] Priya: We'll need metrics on read/write QPS for model checkpoints and KV spill. Typically model weights are resident on local NVMe with prefetching; misses will hit the model shard fetch path. We'll add those parameters into the benchmark plan and bring example perf numbers.

[07:22] Anika: A small hiccup — we have a compliance customer that requires model provenance and model version immutability. Can Redwood pin model versions?
[07:30] Priya: Yes, model pinning and immutable versioning is supported. You can pin to a specific model artifact hash and have rollouts controlled through canary/A-B.
[07:39] Jordan: Also we have a Optimize toolkit that recommends quantization and batching settings by workload — could be useful for your customers to reduce costs without degrading quality.

[07:48] [07:48] Marcus: Nice. Any rough timeline for things if we agree to a pilot next week?
[07:53] Jordan: If you send the inventory and networking details within 2-3 days, we can schedule the deep technical session and aim to standup a baseline pilot in 10–14 days.

[08:00] Lena: That works. Quick question about partner branding: if we offer Redwood as a managed option, can we white-label the API endpoint or do customers need to see Redwood branding?
[08:10] Jordan: We support white-label endpoints and can hide Redwood branding on dashboards for marketplace integrations as part of the partner program. There's a small engineering lead time but it's typical.

[08:20] Marcus: Competitors question — we have customers asking why they'd pick Redwood vs Self-managed with NVIDIA stack or Lambda. What do you tell them?
[08:28] Priya: We emphasize production-grade runtime optimizations (kernel selection, batching, KV management), the unified API across hosted/dedicated/private, and the ops tooling — observability, rollouts, and quality monitoring. Many partners prefer to avoid building and maintaining the serving runtime themselves.

[08:40] Lena: Ok great. Wanna recap next steps?

Recap (auto): Share partner pack + SOC2, send MOU draft, schedule technical deep dive for capacity/benchmarks, Aurora to share inventory and network diagram. Agreed pilot: 1-month, 4x A100 nodes initial, revenue share to be discussed.

[08:55] Jordan: I'll send the partner packet and a draft MOU, Priya will produce a benchmark plan and we'll pick dates with Marcus.
[08:59] Marcus: Thanks. We'll pull together the inventory file and get that to you.
[09:03] Lena: Thanks everyone.
[09:05] Jordan: Thanks all, talk soon.

End transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional timestamps were approximate; some speaker attributions may be generalized (e.g., "Marcus" vs "Speaker 3"). There are minor speech hesitations and overlaps that mimic call audio.
